newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Crime-worried Ireland votes on tightening bail.
newsitem.headline: Crime-worried Ireland votes on tightening bail.

text.p: Ireland votes in a referendum on tightening its bail laws on Thursday in a poll which will pit the nation's liberal conscience against concern that it is riding a crime wave.

Voters will be asked whether to approve or drop a change to the constitution which will allow courts to deny bail to people charged with a serious crime who may commit another offence while awaiting trial.

The change marks a draconian hardening of the current system which allows judges to deny bail only if they fear the suspect will not show up for trial or attempt to interfere with witnesses or evidence.

Prime Minister John Bruton's left-right coalition government, opposition parties and police have thrown their weight behind approving the change because of public outcry over a wave of crime, much of it drug-related.
Official statistics show that the number of crimes committed by people on bail has risen sharply from 2,613 in 1987 to 5,440 in 1995, and figures for this year are expected to show further increases.

The legislation strikes an echo with the public mood over crime which turned to outrage in June when investigative journalist Veronic Guerin was shot dead by a suspected contract killer riding the pillion of a motorbike.
She made her reputation writing about gangland bosses and drug barons living and operating in Ireland and apparently outside the reach of the 10,500-strong police force.
The price of heroin on the streets of Dublin has halved in recent years to around 10 pounds a dose, or the equivalent of four pints of the nation's beloved stout beer.

"Ruthless hardened repeat criminals are walking free from our courts on a daily basis to continue their crime careers and to build up a nest egg during a time on holiday granted by the state," John Durcan of the AGSI police federation said in a statement.

But the proposed change has worried lawyers and civil rights groups who fear that it will effectively mean that a suspect is guilty until proven innocent and jeopardise constitutional guarantees of freedom.
They fear the change will give police arbitrary power to recommend that suspects be denied bail and clog up the nation's already overburdened prisons.
"I shall be voting against it. It is a political gimmick to appease the middle class," said lawyer Andrew Dillon, a member of the criminal litigation council of the Irish Law Society.
Law Society President Frank Daly said he feared the change would lead to a "revolving door" system at prisons under which prisoners would be released early to make way for those denied bail.
"We hear statistics about crimes committed by people on bail but we never hear statistics about crimes committed by people on early release from prison," he said.

Law and Order has already become a campaign issue for a general election due in the next 12 months. The main opposition party, Fianna Fail, has plastered billboards with pictures of two hands grasping iron bars promising that criminals will be put where they belong.
